passages.happening:
“Cry aloud, do not hold back! Raise your voice like a ram’s horn” (verse 1). The prophet is to declare to God's people their sins.

They look eager for God. ‘For day after day they seek Me and delight to know My ways’ (verse 2), as if they were a nation that does what is right. They ask God for righteous judgments and delight in his nearness.

They complain that they have fasted and God has not seen, humbled themselves and he has not noticed (verse 3). God answers. On their fast day they do as they please ‘and you oppress all your workers’ (verse 3). They fast while quarreling and striking with their fists (verse 4). ‘You cannot fast as you do today and have your voice be heard on high’ (verse 4).

Is this the fast God has chosen, a day to bow the head like a reed and lie on sackcloth and ashes (verse 5)?
passages.hearers:
Chapter 57 ended with God's promise to dwell with the contrite. Chapter 58 asks what contrition looks like in practice, and it confronts people who look contrite without being so. The problem here is not open idolatry but religion cut off from justice.

Fasting in Israel meant going without food, often without water, for a day, with sackcloth, ashes on the head and a bowed posture. The law commanded only one fast, on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to humble themselves, and the word for humble in verse 3 is the same word. After the exile, other fasts were kept to remember Jerusalem's fall, and Zechariah records people asking whether to keep them.

Most scholars read the chapter in that setting, a small, struggling community in Judah where, as Nehemiah 5 later describes, wealthier Judeans exploited poorer ones through debt and forced labor. On the traditional view, the same charge fits Isaiah's own day, when he condemned worship without justice in chapter 1.

The ram's horn, the shofar, sounded alarms and announced the Day of Atonement. In Jewish practice this chapter is read in the synagogue on the morning of the Day of Atonement.
passages.later: Zechariah asked the same question of the fasts after the exile: ‘was it really for Me that you fasted?’ (Zechariah 7:5). Jesus warned, ‘When you fast, do not be somber like the hypocrites’ (Matthew 6:16).
passages.asks: The people fasted and oppressed their workers on the same day. Ask whether there is a gap between your worship and the way you treat the people who work for you or serve you. And ask what you expect God to notice about your devotion.

passages.t: The fast God chooses, and light like the dawn
passages.happening:
‘Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke?’ (verse 6). ‘Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood?’ (verse 7).

‘Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will come quickly’ (verse 8). Their righteousness will go before them and the glory of the LORD behind them (verse 8). They will call, and the LORD will answer that he is here (verse 9).

If they remove the yoke, the pointing finger and the malicious talk, and give themselves to the hungry, ‘then your light will go forth in the darkness, and your night will be like noonday’ (verse 10). The LORD will guide them and satisfy them in a scorched land. ‘You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail’ (verse 11). They will rebuild the ancient ruins and be called Repairer of the Breach, Restorer of the Streets of Dwelling (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Verses 6 and 7 turn the complaint around with two questions, each beginning Isn't this the fast. The fast God wants is not less fasting but more: going without exploitation, and sharing the food that was saved.

The yoke was the wooden bar fitted over the necks of oxen, a common picture of oppression and forced labor. To break it meant setting people free from debts and bondage they could not escape.

Verse 7 reaches into the home. The hungry are fed, the homeless brought indoors, the naked clothed, and no one turns from his own flesh and blood.

The promises move from the person to the community: first light and healing, then rebuilt ruins and mended walls. For a people living among ruins, Repairer of the Breach was a name worth having.
passages.later: When Jesus announced his mission at Nazareth, the reading from Isaiah includes a line from verse 6, ‘to release the oppressed’ (Luke 4:18). James describes the same faith: pure religion is ‘to care for orphans and widows in their distress’ (James 1:27).
passages.asks: The fast God chooses is to share bread and open the home. Ask whom in your own family or neighborhood you have turned away from. And ask what breach in your community you could help repair.

passages.happening: ‘If you turn your foot from breaking the Sabbath, from doing as you please on My holy day, if you call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD’s holy day honorable’ (verse 13). They are to honor it by not going their own way, seeking their own pleasure or speaking idle words. Then the promise: ‘then you will delight yourself in the LORD’ (verse 14). God will make them ride on the heights of the land and feed them with the inheritance of their father Jacob. ‘For the mouth of the LORD has spoken’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The Sabbath was the weekly day of rest commanded in the law. It also protected servants and workers from endless labor, so it belongs with the rest of the chapter. A people who oppressed their workers on their fast days would not keep a day that gave those workers rest.

The verses turn on a play on the word delight, oneg. Those who stop chasing their own delight on God's day will find their delight in the LORD. In Jewish tradition, oneg Shabbat, the delight of the Sabbath, became a name for the joy of keeping the day.

The promise reaches back to Jacob. The inheritance of the ancestors, the land itself, is fed to those who rest.
passages.later: The law gave the day for rest ‘so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do’ (Deuteronomy 5:14). Jesus said, ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath’ (Mark 2:27).
passages.asks: God calls the Sabbath a delight, not a burden. Ask whether you have a day you treat as a delight in the LORD. And ask who works so that you can rest, and whether they rest too.
